title: Basic Sentence
subtitle: SVO word order
explanation: The most basic sentence structure can simply consist of two to three words. The order in which Subj., Verb and Obj. are named is the same as in English (SVO).

sentences.translation: You come here!
I go to school.
What place do you want to go to?

title: Connect Noun and Adjective with 很
explanation:
很 [hěn] is used to connect a Noun to an Adjective. The adverb is used as a verb ('is') to describe the Subject of the sentence. To translate sentences of this particular structure, you can't rely on the original meaning of 很 ('very').

The meaning of 很 is retained in questions and negative statements that follow the same sentence structure.

To connect Noun with Noun the Verb 是 [shì] is used instead.

sentences.translation: He is tall.
He is very tall.
Are they very busy?
They are not very busy.
They are busy.

title: Connect Nouns with 是
explanation:
是 [shì] is only used to link two nouns. The chinese language does not conjugate verbs, so it never changes based on gender or numbers. 

To link adjectives, 是 is replaced by 很 [hěn].

sentences.translation: What food is that?

sentences.pronunciation: wǒ yě shì nǐ de péngyou.
sentences.translation: I'm also your friend.
I am Ming Suli.

title: Coordinating Conjunction for Nouns
subtitle: A and B
explanation:
和 [hé] is used to link nouns or pronouns. 

It is not used to link verbs or sentences. For those cases we use 也 [yě].

sentences.pronunciation: déyǔ hé hànyǔ dōu hěn nán.
sentences.translation: German and Chinese are both difficult.

sentences.text: 我妈妈，爸爸和我啊hi一个家挺。
sentences.pronunciation: wǒ māma, bàba hé wǒ shì yī gè jiātìng.
sentences.translation: My mother, father and I live together.

sentences.pronunciation: jīntiān hé míngtiān dōu kěyǐ ma?
sentences.translation: Are today and tomrrow both OK?

title: Excessive Adjectives
explanation:
In Chinese, the simplest structure for expressing 'too' in the sense of 'excessively' is by using the word 太 [tài].
Don't forget to also add 了 [le] after the adjective to keep your Chinese sounding natural.

In case of a positive adjective (好吃, 好看), 太 [tài] is translated as "very" or "so". This is to express satisfaction. On the other hand, in combination with an adjective that can have a negative meaning (热, 冷), the translation becomes more of a complaint because it's too much.

sentences.translation: The noodles were so good.
There is too much rice. It's too much
You are so great.
He is so handsome.
It's too hot today.

title: Negation
subtitle: Standard negation with 不 in the present
explanation:
不 [bù] is generally used to negate a verb in the present or future, or to talk about what you do not do, as a habit. So expressing things like "I don't want to go" or "I'm not going" or "I don't eat meat" would be typical uses. The only verb that can never be negated with 不 [bù] is 有 [yǒu].

Adjectives can also be negated. This indicates a current state of being. The 很 [hěn] disappears.

sentences.translation: They are not bad kids.
We don't drink alcohol.
I'm not hungry.
This is not expensive.
The boss is very unhappy today.

title: Questions with Options
subtitle: A or B
structures: Subj. + Verb + [Option A] + 还是 + [Option B]?
explanation:
The 还是 [háishì] in a question represents 'or'. It is used to ask for a choice between two or more options.

There are other ways to ask between more than two options involving 你要哪个? (Which one do you want?).

sentences.translation: Me or him?
Do you want tea or coffee?

sentences.pronunciation: là de háishì bù là de?
sentences.translation: Spicy or non-spicy?

title: Questions with 不
subtitle: Affirmative-negative question with 不
explanation:
A common way to form questions in Chinese is to first use a verb in the positive, then repeat the same verb in its negative form. It can also be done with adjectives.

These compositons are often used as tag questions at the end of a sentence.

The only exception to the case is 没 [méi] because that verb is never negated with 不 [bù].

sentences.translation: Are you coming back home or not?
Is it good?
Does your dad drink alcohol or not?

sentences.pronunciation: Zhèlǐ de kāfēi gùi bu gùi?
sentences.translation: Is the coffee expensive here?
Is Chinese food spicy?

sentences.pronunciation: Nǐ huì shuō Zhōngwén, duì bu duì?
sentences.translation: You speak Chinese, right?

sentences.pronunciation: Tā shì nǐ de lǎobǎn, duì bu duì?
sentences.translation: He's your boss, right?

sentences.text: 你有新女朋友了，是不是？
sentences.pronunciation: Nǐ yǒu xīn nǚpéngyou le, shì bu shì?
sentences.translation: You have a new girlfriend, right?

title: Questions with 吗
subtitle: Tag questions with 吗
explanation:
Tag questions are quick questions that are tagged on the end of a sentence to ask for confirmation. 
Examples of that in English are 'OK?' or 'right?' . In Chinese 吗 [ma] is typically used with certain verbs or adjectives to form tag questions. Prominent examples are: 是 [shì], 可以 [kěyǐ], 对 [duì], 好 [hǎo].

sentences.pronunciation: nǐ méi lái guo, shì ma?
sentences.translation: You haven't been here, right?
Don't tell him, OK?

title: Questions with 吗
subtitle: Yes/no questions with 吗
explanation:
Any statement can be converted into a yes/no question by adding a 吗 [ma] at the end. 

To answer yes/no questions you can use the verbs within the question or 对 [duì] as a general term.

sentences.translation: Do you like coffee? Yes
Are you also going? No

sentences.pronunciation: nǐ míngtiān bù lái ma? lái
sentences.translation: You're not coming tomorrow? Yes, I'll come.

title: Questions with 呢
subtitle: Reciprocal questions with 呢
explanation:
By combining a topic with 呢 [ne], you can basically ask about anything you want. Typically this is used to ask 'What about ...?' which in some cases can be interpreted as 'Where is ...?'.

Topics can be persons, places, things, time points, etc.

sentences.translation: I'm home. What about you?

sentences.text: 今天晚上没空？明天晚上呢？
sentences.pronunciation: jīntiān wǎnshang méi kòng? míngtiān wǎnshang ne?
sentences.translation: You don't have time tonight? What about tomorrow evening?
This one is good. What about that one?
It's raining in Beijing. How about in Shanghai?
Where's my cell phone?
Where's your mom?

title: Structure of Dates
subtitle: Dates in spoken Mandarin
structures: 年 + y 月 + z 号  (spoken)
opposite_structures: 年 + y 月 + z 日  (written)
explanation: Dates 年月号 are arranged from largest unit to smallest: year, month, day.

sentences.pronunciation: Nǐ de shēngrì shì shíyīyuè shíyī hào ma?
sentences.translation: Is your birthday November 11th?
January 1st is New Year's Day.

sentences.pronunciation: Yī-jiǔ-bā-líng nián Jiǔyuè sì hào wǒmen jiéhūn le.
sentences.translation: We got married on September 4th, 1980.

title: Structure of Dates
subtitle: Dates in written Mandarin
structures: 年 + y 月 + z 日  (written)
opposite_structures: 年 + y 月 + z 号  (spoken)
explanation: Dates 年月日 are arranged from largest unit to smallest: year, month, day.

sentences.pronunciation: nǐ de shēngrì shì shíyīyuè shíyī hào ma?
sentences.translation: Is your birthday November 11th?
January 1st is New Year's Day.

sentences.pronunciation: yī-jiǔ-bā-líng nián jiǔyuè sì hào wǒmen jiéhūn le.
sentences.translation: We got married on September 4th, 1980.

title: Structure of Numbers
subtitle: Numbers from 0 to 9999
structures: a + 千 + b + 百 + c + 十 + d
explanation:
Chinese handles numbers in a very consistent and logical way. All the tens are also formed very logically. Twenty is 二十 [èrshí], thirty is 三十 [sānshí], and so on.

Note: when there's a '0' in the middle of a number, you read it as 零 [líng], and don't put a unit (like 'ten' or 'hundred') after it.

For numbers greater than 1, if the number ends in zero 11, 23, 3, 4, etc.], a number like 150 can be read as 一百五十 [yībǎi wǔshí], but is often read as 一百五 [yībǎi wǔ]. In fact, reading it as 一百五 [yībǎi wǔ] always means 150, never 105. As described above, 105 would be read as 一百零五 [yībǎi líng wǔ].

千 [qiān] means 'thousand' in Chinese. Its rules of usage are similar to the rules for 'hundred'. Just note that no matter how many zeroes are in the middle of the number, you just say 零 [líng] once.

Chinese phone numbers are given as a string of individual numbers, using the digits 0-9. The only trick is that the number 1 is often pronounced 'yāo' instead of 'yī' to avoid confusion with number 7, which is pronounced 'qī'.

sentences.pronunciation: yāo sān wǔ líng yāo èr líng líng yāo èr líng
sentences.translation: (as phone number)

characters: 一…二…三…四…五…六…七…八…九…十
一二三四五六七八九十

title: Uncertainty with 吧
subtitle: Shift from Declarative to Interrogative
explanation:
吧 [ba] is a modal particle and as such is used to 
express the mood, attitude, or tone in a sentence.
Generally, 吧 has many functions, but they all seem to shift the feel of a sentence to be less forceful / certain.

吧 can be placed in the end of a declarative sentence to turn it into a yes/no question, in order to express a doubt. In this pattern, 吧 [ba] functions the same as 吗 [ma], used in yes/no questions. 吧 is used when the speaker expects an affirmative answer to the question. 吗 is used when the speaker genuinely does not know the answer and wants to find out.

title: Coordinating Conjunction
subtitle: A or B
explanation:
或者 [huòzhě] expresses 'or' between two statements. 

This is not used in questions. For that, 还是 [háishì] is typically used.

sentences.pronunciation: wǒ hē shuǐ huòzhě chá, dōu xíng.
sentences.translation: I drink water or tea. Either is fine.

title: Correlative Conjunction for Adjectives
subtitle: Both A and B
structures: Subj. + 又 + Adj. + 又 + Adj.
explanation: When you're getting descriptive, you may find yourself wanting to use multiple adjectives at a time. The character 又 [yòu] can be used to give two qualities to something. Using the double 又 [yòu] structure is like saying that something is 'both A and B' in English.

sentences.translation: Her boyfriend is both tall and handsome.
This house is both big and bright.
Mom's hair is both black and shiny.
My older sister is both smart and beautiful.
Chinese food is both cheap and good-tasting.

sentences.text: 你们老板又年轻又有钱。
sentences.translation: Your boss is both young and rich.

sentences.text: 这里的咖啡又贵又难喝。
sentences.translation: The coffee here is both expensive and bad-tasting.

sentences.text: 我家小狗又可爱又听话。
sentences.translation: My family's dog is both cute and obedient.
Shanghai's winter is both cold and humid.
She was both short and thin when she was young.

title: Quantity questions
subtitle: Measure words in quantity questions with 几
explanation: You can use the quantity question word 几 [jǐ] instead of a number to ask about quantity with measure words.

sentences.translation: How many kids does he have?

sentences.pronunciation: nǐ jiā yǒu jǐ gè fángjiān?
sentences.translation: How many rooms are there in your house?

sentences.text: 他们在这里住几个星期？
sentences.pronunciation: Tāmen zài zhèlǐ zhù jǐ gè xīngqī?
sentences.translation: How many weeks are they staying here?
How many pieces of clothing have you brought?

sentences.text: 老板每天工作几个小时？
sentences.pronunciation: Lǎobǎn měi tiān gōngzuò jǐ gè xiǎoshí?
sentences.translation: How many hours does the boss work every day?
How many sisters are there in your family?

title: Reluctant Agreement with 吧
subtitle: Shift from Assertive to Concessive
explanation:
吧 [ba] is a modal particle and as such is used to 
express the mood, attitude, or tone in a sentence.
Generally, 吧 has many functions, but they all seem to shift the feel of a sentence to be less forceful / certain.

You can place 吧 at the end of a statement to show agreement which you are not really happy about but have to accept.

title: Result Complement 到
subtitle: Listening vs hearing with 听 and 到
explanation:
The result complement 到 [dào] is used to indicate that the action the verb is describing has achieved an outcome. Without the complement, the sentence would describe only the action itself. In the negative form no outcome has been achieved.

■ 听 [tīng] = listening 
■ 听到 [tīngdào] = hearing, processing the information
■ 没听到 [méitīngdào] = did't hear
■ 听不到 [tīngbudào] = can't hear

Based on the choice of complement, the indication as to what the result is can slightly change.  
Other complement forms are: 听见, 听说

sentences.translation: Did you hear it?
You didn't hear it?
I heard your voice.
I didn't hear a knock on the door.

sentences.text: 什么声音？我怎么没听到？
sentences.pronunciation: shénme shēngyīn? wǒ zěnme méi tīngdào?
sentences.translation: What noise? Why didn't I hear it?
Listen now!
You hear no birds here.

sentences.text: 他一听到风信就赶去了。
sentences.pronunciation: tā yī tīngdào fēngxìn jiù gǎnqùle.
sentences.translation: As soon as he got wind of it, he went at once.

sentences.text: 听到这个消息，她就安心了。
sentences.pronunciation: tīngdào zhège xiōxi, tā jì n1xn1le.
sentences.translation: She was relieved at the news.

title: Result Complement 到
subtitle: Looking vs seeing with 看 and 到
explanation:
The result complement 到 [dào] is used to indicate that the action the verb is describing has achieved an outcome. Without the complement, the sentence would describe only the action itself. In the negative form, no outcome has been achieved.

■ 听 [kàn] = use eyes (look/read/watch) 
■ 听到 [kàndào] = see (incl. abstract concepts)
■ 听不到 [kànbudào] = can't see 
■ 没听到 [méikàndào] = didn't see

Based on the choice of complement, the indication as to what the result is can slightly change. 
Other complement forms are: 看见, 看说

sentences.text: 我看到了你光明的未来。
sentences.pronunciation: wǒ kàndàole nǐ guāngmíng de wèilái.
sentences.translation: I see a bright future for you.

sentences.text: 我没看到的，你都看到了，真是面面俱到。
sentences.pronunciation: wǒ méi kàndào de, nǐ dōu kàndàole, zhēnshi miànmiànjùdào.
sentences.translation: You saw everything I missed. You really covered everything.

sentences.text: 我看到了你语言能力的提高。
sentences.pronunciation: wǒ kàndàole nǐ yǔyánnénglì de tígāo.
sentences.translation: I can see the improvement in your language skills.

sentences.text: 她太矮了，看不到圍牆外面。
sentences.pronunciation: tā tài ǎile, kàn bu dào wéiqiáng wàimian.
sentences.translation: She was too short to see over the fence.

sentences.text: 我们看不到月亮的另一边。
sentences.pronunciation: wǒmen kàn bu dào yuèliang de lìngyībiān
sentences.translation: We can't see the other side of the moon.

title: Result Complement 见
subtitle: Listening vs hearing with 听 and 见
explanation:
The result complement 见 [jiàn] is used to indicate that the action the verb is describing has achieved an outcome. Without the complement, the sentence would describe only the action itself. In the negative form no outcome has been achieved.

■ 听 [tīng] = listening 
■ 听见 [tīngjiàn] = (physically) hearing
■ 没听见 [méitīngjiàn] = didn't hear
■ 听不见 [tīngbujiàn] = can't hear

Based on the choice of complement, the indication as to what the result is can slightly change.  
Other complement forms are: 听到, 听说

sentences.translation: I heard a loud noise.
I can't hear the noise.
I heard a knock at the door.

sentences.pronunciation: hǎoxiàng shéi yě méi tīngjiàn líng xiǎng.
sentences.translation: No one seems to have heard the bell.
Not a sound was heard.
I can hear strange noises.
You didn't hear it?
Did you hear what I said?
It's not loud enough. I can't hear you.

sentences.pronunciation: wǒ méi tīngjiàn. shēngyīn búgòu dà.
sentences.translation: I didn't hear you. It wasn't loud enough.

sentences.text: 我听了一会儿，可什么也没听见。
sentences.pronunciation: wǒ tīngle yíhuir!, kě shénme yě méi tīngjiàn.
sentences.translation: I listened for a while, but heard nothing.
I like listening to the radio.
He's hard of hearing and can't hear you.

title: Result Complement 见
subtitle: Looking vs seeing with 看 and 见
explanation:
The result complement 见 [jiàn] is used to indicate that the action the verb is describing has achieved an outcome. Without the complement, the sentence would describe only the action itself. In the negative form no outcome has been achieved.

■ 听 [kàn] = use eyes (look/read/watch)  
■ 听见 [kànjiàn] = see (incl. abstract concepts) 
■ 听不见 [kànbujiàn] = can't see 
■ 没听见 [méikànjiàn] = didn't see

Based on the choice of complement, the indication as to what the result is can slightly change. 
Other complement forms are: 看到, 看说

sentences.text: 你看见我的手机了吗？没看见。
sentences.pronunciation: nǐ kànjàin wǒde shǒujǐle ma? méi kànjiàn.
sentences.translation: Have you seen my cell phone? No, I haven't.
Did you see that handsome guy?

sentences.pronunciation: nǐ méi kànjiàn nàge shuàigē ma?
sentences.translation: You didn't see that handsome guy?
I saw it.
I didn't see it.

sentences.text: 我在暗中什么也看不见。
sentences.pronunciation: wǒ zài ànzhōng shénme yě kàn bu jiàn.
sentences.translation: I couldn't see anything in the dark.
Bacteria are invisible to the naked eye.

title: Result Complement 说
subtitle: Listening vs hearing with 听 and 说
structures: Subj. + 听 + Source + 说 + Obj.
explanation:
The result complement 说 [shūo] is used to indicate that the action the verb is describing has achieved an outcome. Without the complement, the sentence would describe only the action itself. In the negative form no outcome has been achieved.

■ 听 [tīng] = listening 
■ 听说 [tīngshūo] = hear of, to be told
■ 没听说 [méitīngshūo] = haven't heard of

Based on the choice of complement, the indication as to what the result is can slightly change. 
Other complement forms are: 听见, 听到

sentences.translation: I heard you're getting married.

sentences.text: 我怎么没听说过这事儿？
sentences.pronunciation: wǒ zěnme méi tīngshuō guò zhè shìr.
sentences.translation: How come I never heard of it?

sentences.text: 我听说这首歌现在很流行。
sentences.pronunciation: wǒ tīngshuō zhè shǒu gē xiànzài hěn liúxíng.
sentences.translation: I heard this song is very popular right now.
Never heard of it.

sentences.pronunciation: wǒ hái méi tīngshuō guò tā?
sentences.translation: I haven't heard of him yet.

sentences.text: 听新闻说下个星期会下大雨。
sentences.pronunciation: tīng xīnwén xiàgèxīngqī huì xià dàyǔ.
sentences.translation: I heard on the news it's going to rain heavily next week.
who told you that?

title: Suggestion with 吧
subtitle: Shift from Imperative to Suggestive
explanation:
吧 [ba] is a modal particle and as such is used to 
express the mood, attitude, or tone in a sentence.
Generally, 吧 has many functions, but they all seem to shift the feel of a sentence to be less forceful / certain. 

One example is the shift from imperative to suggestive. The modal particle shifts the commanding statement to a much more polite suggestion or request.

title: Emphasizing Negation with 又
subtitle: Intensify negation with 没 or 不
explanation:
In this structure, 又 [yòu] is used to emphasize that something definitely 'didn't happen', 'is not the case', or 'will not happen'. It's most often used with 不 [bù] and 没 [méi]. 

This grammar structure is often used in an accusatory context, and when used with other expressions like 干吗 [gànmá] can show annoyance.

sentences.translation: He is absent from the class again.
He refuses to be present in class again.

sentences.pronunciation: wèn wǒ gànmá? wǒ yòu bù zhīdào.
sentences.translation: Why ask me? I definitely don't know.

sentences.text: 这些菜又没坏，为什么要扔？
sentences.pronunciation: zhèxiē cài yòu méi huài, wèishénme yào rēng?
sentences.translation: These dishes haven't gone bad. Why would you throw them away?

sentences.pronunciation: yòu méi xiàyǔ, dài sǎn gànmá?
sentences.translation: It's not raining. Why are you bringing the umbrella?

sentences.text: 不要生气，我又不是故意的。
sentences.pronunciation: bùyào shēngqì, wǒ yòu bù shì gùyì de.
sentences.translation: Don't be mad. It really wasn't on purpose.

sentences.text: 你现在又不忙，来帮我一下。
sentences.pronunciation: nǐ xiànzài yòu bù máng, lái bāng wǒ yīxià.
sentences.translation: You're not busy now. Come and help me.

title: Repetition of Past Action with 又
subtitle: Expresses repetition of a previous action in the immediate future
structures: Subj. + 又 + Aux. + Verb + Obj. (+ 了) (repetition will happen immediately)
opposite_structures: Subj. + 又 + Verb + 了 (repetition has happened)
explanation:
又 [yòu] is sometimes used to express that something that has happened before is going to happen in the immediate future and has not happened yet. It usually appears with 要 [yào], 可以 [kěyǐ], 能 [néng], 是 [shì], or 得 [děi]. This usage often expresses exasperation or impatience with something happening yet again, but sometimes it's more neutral, or even happy.

For general repetition of an action in the future, 再 is usually used.

sentences.text: 老板请客，又可以吃大餐了。
sentences.pronunciation: lǎobǎn qǐngkè, yòu kěyǐ chī dàcān le.
sentences.translation: The boss is going to treat us. We can have a big meal again!

sentences.text: 夏天快到了，又可以吃冰淇淋了。
sentences.pronunciation: lǎobǎn qǐngkè, yòu kěyǐ chī dàcān le.
sentences.translation: It's almost summer, and we can eat ice cream again!

sentences.text: 昨天银行关门，事情没办成，今天又得请假去银行了。。
sentences.pronunciation: xiàtiān kuài dào le, yòu kěyǐ chī bīngqílín le
sentences.translation: Yesterday the bank was closed and things were not done. Today, I have to ask for leave to go to the bank again.

sentences.text: 快过年了，我们又能拿红包了。
sentences.pronunciation: kuài guònián le, wǒmen yòu néng ná hóngbāo le.
sentences.translation: It's almost Chinese New Year. We can get our red packets [of money] again!
Tomorrow is Monday again.

sentences.text: 今年备不住又是个丰收年。
sentences.translation: This year may be another good year.
It rained again.
You're late again.
The baby is crying again.
I forgot again.
This guy is here again.

sentences.pronunciation: wǒ zuótiān yòu chī huǒguō le.
sentences.translation: I ate hot pot again yesterday.

title: Repetition of Past Action with 又
subtitle: Expresses repetition of an action that has already occurred in the past
structures: Subj. + 又 + Verb + 了 (repetition has happened)
opposite_structures: Subj. + 又 + Aux. + Verb + Obj. (+ 了) (repetition will happen immediately)
explanation:
又 [yòu] is used in declarative sentences and describes the simple repetition of actions. This repeated action has already occurred once in the past. It doesn't have to be in quick succession. It happened before, and now it's happened again. 
再  [hái] and 还  [zài] can be used to indicate 'again' or repeating a previous action.

sentences.translation: It rained again.
You're late again.
The baby is crying again.
I forgot again.
This guy is here again.

sentences.pronunciation: wǒ zuótiān yòu chī huǒguō le.
sentences.translation: I ate hot pot again yesterday.

sentences.text: 上个星期妈妈又生气了。
sentences.translation: Mom was angry again last week.

sentences.text: 你怎么又给我打电话了？什么事？
sentences.pronunciation: nǐ zěnme yòu gěi wǒ dǎ diànhuà le? shénme shì?
sentences.translation: Why do you keep calling me? What it it?

sentences.text: 你为什么又看这本书了你？已经看过了。
sentences.pronunciation: nǐ wèishénme yòu kàn zhèběnshū le nǐ? yǐjīng kànguòle.
sentences.translation: Why are you reading that book again？You've already read it.

sentences.text: 老板请客，又可以吃大餐了。
sentences.pronunciation: lǎobǎn qǐngkè, yòu kěyǐ chī dàcān le.
sentences.translation: The boss is going to treat us. We can have a big meal again!

sentences.text: 夏天快到了，又可以吃冰淇淋了。
sentences.pronunciation: lǎobǎn qǐngkè, yòu kěyǐ chī dàcān le.
sentences.translation: It's almost summer, and we can eat ice cream again!

sentences.text: 昨天银行关门，事情没办成，今天又得请假去银行了。。
sentences.pronunciation: xiàtiān kuài dào le, yòu kěyǐ chī bīngqílín le
sentences.translation: Yesterday the bank was closed and things were not done. Today, I have to ask for leave to go to the bank again.
Tomorrow is Monday again.

sentences.text: 今年备不住又是个丰收年。
sentences.translation: This year may be another good year.

sentences.text: 快过年了，我们又能拿红包了。
sentences.pronunciation: kuài guònián le, wǒmen yòu néng ná hóngbāo le.
sentences.translation: It's almost Chinese New Year. We can get our red packets (of money) again!
